aiSummary: Photography is profoundly consequential for Józef Sarnowski, born 28 August 1862, as it exposes the tension between his continuous embodied self and institutions perceiving him through contradictory public records. This phenomenon, framed as ‘identity against documentation’ and linked to ‘factical thickening,’ emerges from photography’s role in binding individuals into dense networks of public references like passports and archives. Phenomenologically, photography creates a fracture between lived body and photographed body, echoing Merleau-Ponty’s view of the body as central to experience, exacerbated by Józef’s aristocratic temperament and control. The transition from portrait-based self-possession to a world where images circulate without permission marks a critical historical shift. Temporality is equally disrupted: Józef’s inner life evolves steadily while his outward appearance remains stable, making 1907 photographs dangerously accurate for collapsing assumptions of familial resemblance. Barthes’ *Camera Lucida* and the *punctum* concept highlight how subtle details trigger pre-reflective recognition, while Heidegger’s analysis of mortality underscores the pain of preserving unchanged lives against personal longevity. Photographs become ‘fixed islands’ of past worlds, serving both as painful reminders and a private form of mourning for the one who persists beyond them.
title: Photography and Józef Sarnowski
